title: Wimy: What's in My Room Interior Planner
pitch: Less clicks, more possibilities of what goes into your room
about_excerpt: Less clicks, more possibilities of what goes into your room Like Comment Story Updates 2D room plan with dimensions, openings, furniture, and orientation 3D preview with location-aware lighting. WebMCP agent trace: inspect, place, and verify with revision-safe edits Inspiration Two problems for the ones trying to decorate their space, either moving in or just revamping: Finding a good piece of furniture that you, yes you , would like, based on your preferences. Making sure they fit within constraints of area and $. What it does Wimy is a website that contains a catalog of furniture, with the main UI showing the placement of the selected piece(s) of furniture going in the room as 2D from-the-top model and also 3D rendering of how they fit in space. The current demo uses fictional furniture and models we created ourselves. Moreover, the 3D rendering also shows how it would look based on the approximate location (e.g., New York vs Hong Kong) at a certain time of the day with sunlight and moonlight. Think of it as when you are buying furniture in the Sims. The key WebMCP value is that the agent can read the room’s structured state and act on it. Instead of guessing from screenshots or clicks, it can inspect dimensions and openings, search for furniture that fits, apply one revision-safe edit, and report the result while the person reviews the visual design and makes changes too. The room becomes a shared workspace between the person and the agent. One more thing is that we come up with a format to share the output so in the case where one is sharing the design with their friend, they can just give them the .wimy file. Essentially, it is a JSON of the details of the design that can be imported and exported. How we built it Starting from the furniture/catalog data and 2D room geometry, Wimy is a React/TypeScript Vite app. Incrementally, we started to add more features to ensure that the goal that it can deliver a full experience of furniture placement in their room with rendering, all enhanced by WebMCP. The additional features are Lighting: approximate sunlight and moonlight based on location, date, time, and room orientation, with a slider to explore the day. Atomic human/agent edits: changes are validated against the current revision and either applied completely or rejected, so an agent cannot overwrite a newer edit. Portable designs: .wimy files preserve room geometry, furniture references, and placements without requiring an account. Catalog search and substitutes: filter furniture by style, price, and dimensions, then compare alternatives that fit. Then, WebMCP tools are registered through navigator.modelContext for the tools listed below: inspect_room : read the room’s revision, dimensions, furniture, openings, and warnings. find_furniture : search the catalog for furniture that fits the room and preferences. apply_room_edit : add, move, rotate, or remove furniture. apply_room_structure_edit : rename the room, adjust dimensions and supported shapes, and edit doors and windows. inspect_lighting_preview : read the current lighting settings. set_lighting_preview : change location, date, time, and orientation. inspect_retailer_offers : inspect synthetic offers for a catalog item. inspect_room_shopping_plan : compare synthetic offers grouped by retailer for the room’s items. find_substitutes : suggest comparable furniture and explain fit and tradeoffs. With the appropriate signed-in permissions, inspect_cart , find_retailer_offers , add_to_cart , and remove_from_cart manage provider selections for the room’s shopping plan. These are demo capabilities; real checkout is not connected. Lastly, the UI renders 2D and a lazy procedural 3D preview and deploys as a public static site on Vercel. Challenges we ran into Initially, the challenge lies in choosing the UI format that would make it usable, to which we found IKEA Kreativ as a good inspiration for the UI layout during our research phase. Then, the main challenges outstanding are Lack of items in the catalog and metadata for each of them. In this case, we wanted to be on the safer side and not scrape models of furnitures with copyrights. Lighting in 3D rendering are still not solid. Specifically, the ray of light are still somewhat a rectangular ray and uniform which might not be like something out of Blender or Unreal Engine. Integration into other marketplaces is tricky since we wanted Wimy to be the planner and the user can just go and finish their checkout at IKEA or other vendors, which it would resolve challenge #1 as well (i.e., full access and integrations to other vendors). Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud to come up with the shareable data format so that the user can share their design with their peers. Moreover, we are also proud of the rendering which enhance the UX; thus, answering the question of "how would this sofa look like in my room". Lastly, the part we are most proud of is registering WebMCP tools and being able to let the agent use preferences from our conversation, such as "I like European-styled furniture" and the tools to let the agents do the work in an efficient manner for us, since it might find some rare finds assuming the catalog was extensive. What we learned We learned that 3D rendering and lighting rendering especially, are hard. Also, I learned that there are more layers to democratizing the vendors into having a one-stop shop for designing and fitting pieces and parts in your room (e.g., checking the license and permissions before reusing a vendor’s models). What's next for Wimy: What's in My Room Interior Planner We were thinking that we would integrate Agentic Commerce Protocol and wire it to WebMCP to allow buying the pieces you planned on the UI using agents. In addition, if we can ask other vendors like IKEA or Wayfair to join us in this endeavor then we can split the bill by paying only for IKEA for items from IKEA. In this case, we already include provider metadata in catalog packages, while .wimy files preserve the design and catalog references. We also want to support richer room footprints, including U-shaped rooms. We also want to support richer room footprints, including U-shaped rooms.
